pgb1q29-d1e3115.summary: Opens the exposition of distinction 37 ('Et quoniam demonstratum est'). Having treated how things exist in God's knowledge, Lombard now shows how God is in the essence of every creature. Gracilis divides the distinction into three parts. The first recounts modes of God's being in things and approves the true ones. The second rejects false modes (c. 5, 'cumque divina natura'). The third confirms the teaching (c. 9, 'fateamur itaque').
claims: Distinction 37 moves from things' being in God's knowledge to God's being in things.
It divides into approval of true modes, refutation of false modes, and confirmation.

pgb1q29-d1e3138.summary: Subdivides the first part. Lombard first shows how God is specially in some things through grace, then how he is generally in things through nature. The part on grace is itself divided into the claim that God dwells in holy persons and replies to doubts about it.
claims: God is in some things specially by grace and in all things generally by nature.

pgb1q29-d1e3163.summary: States the question in two formulations. Is the divine, necessary principle necessarily in every being? And as God is the true and infallible idea of every thing, is every thing likewise a place capable of God, though mutable? The question links the preceding treatment of divine ideas to divine omnipresence.

pgb1q29-qnqsee.summary: First principal argument for the negative. If God were everywhere, nothing would be locally distant from him, and he could not act on a distant patient. But acting at a distance is possible, since agents act sooner on near than on far things. Confirmation: God can be everywhere by power without being everywhere by essence.
claims: God can be everywhere by power without being everywhere by essence.

pgb1q29-d1e3213.summary: Second principal argument. God can acquire a new place, being in a place or creature where he previously was not. So he is not immutably in every place. Also, since no creature exists necessarily, some being might not be God's place.
claims: God can come to be where he was not.
No creature is necessary, so no creature is necessarily God's place.

pgb1q29-d1e3229.summary: Third principal argument: God is not present everywhere. If God destroyed and recreated every place, he would begin to be everywhere. God is not in the imagined void. And the God-man is not everywhere, since as man he would then be a body in infinitely many places, so God is not everywhere.
claims: God's ubiquity can begin and so is not necessary.
Christ as man is not everywhere.

pgb1q29-d1e3257.summary: Sed contra: the Master's teaching in this distinction, confirmed by the argument that being everywhere is a perfection and so must be attributed to God.
claims: Ubiquity is a perfection and so belongs to God.

pgb1q29-d1e3271.summary: First conclusion: God cannot be in any created thing by his power without being in it by his essence. Lombard's statement that being everywhere is proper to the deity supports it. Gracilis adds Giles of Rome's qualification (De corpore Christi, theorem 5) that God, though in every place, is not determined, defined, or circumscribed by place.
claims: God's presence by power entails his presence by essence.
God is in every place without being determined, defined, or circumscribed by place.

pgb1q29-d1e3309.summary: First corollary, against Scotus. If divine power is absent from no being or place, it follows sufficiently that the divine essence is everywhere, because power and essence in God are identical.
claims: Divine power and essence are identical, so ubiquity of power entails ubiquity of essence.

pgb1q29-d1e3321.summary: Second corollary. A created agent can act on something at a distance, as the sun lights and heats distant air. The uncreated agent cannot act on anything distant from itself, because God is intimately present to every being and site.
claims: Creatures can act at a distance.
God cannot act at a distance because nothing is distant from him.

pgb1q29-d1e3339.summary: Third corollary, distinguishing two kinds of ubiquity. Being present to every place attinctive, by reaching it through power and essence, belongs properly to God alone. A mutable creature could be everywhere contentive, by being in the only place there is: if every place but mine were annihilated, I would be everywhere.
claims: Ubiquity 'attinctive' is proper to God.
A creature could be everywhere 'contentive' if all other places were annihilated.

pgb1q29-d1e3363.summary: Second conclusion. As God needs no created place for his being, so no place determinately contains him. Needing a place is the condition of a located thing. To be properly contained by a place is to be bounded and exceeded by it, and no place can bound or exceed God.
claims: God needs no place for his existence.
No place contains God, since containment means being bounded and exceeded.

pgb1q29-d1e3375.summary: First corollary. Place, time, and situs are said of God only by transference, as Augustine says (De Trin. V). Even so, the modes of God's being in creatures are really distinguished. Following Gerard of Siena: being in by essence is reaching the other's essence with no intervening distance (which supports the second corollary of the first conclusion); being in by presence is reaching it by knowledge and foreknowledge; being in by power is being in it through conserving operation.
claims: Spatial and temporal predicates apply to God only translatively.
God is in things by essence, by presence, and by power, and these modes are distinct.

pgb1q29-d1e3420.summary: Second corollary. It is as impossible for God to be defined by place, moved, or changed as for a creature to exist without God being intimately present to it. Augustine is cited: there would be no mutable goods without an immutable good. Being defined by a place means the place bounds and exceeds what it locates.
claims: Creatures cannot exist without God's intimate presence.
God cannot be defined by place, moved, or changed.

pgb1q29-d1e3451.summary: Third corollary. God is in himself in one way, immutably, but in creatures in many ways, because 'God is in creatures' connotes his diverse effects in them, which differ in rational and brute creatures. Alan of Lille's Regulae 38–39 support this: ubiquity-talk predicates God's immensity, not circumscription. 'God is in every place' signifies immensity, 'God is in the saints' signifies the conferral of grace, and 'God is in the assumed man' signifies union.
claims: God's being in creatures connotes his effects in them.
Spatial predications of God signify immensity, grace, or hypostatic union.

pgb1q29-d1e3520.summary: Third conclusion. It is necessary that God be in every created thing, since nothing can exist without God conserving it and being intimately present to it. Yet God is in this body or place contingently, since this place could be annihilated.
claims: God is necessarily in whatever creature exists.
God's being in any particular place is contingent.

pgb1q29-d1e3545.summary: First corollary. God is necessarily in whatever exists while it exists, and is truly in nothing that does not exist. Otherwise the non-existent would both be and not be, since God's being in something is his reaching it by essence, knowledge, and operation.
claims: God is in nothing that does not exist.
concepts: presence by essence, knowledge and operation

pgb1q29-d1e3563.summary: Second corollary. As no place can exist with God absent from it, so nothing non-existent can have God present to it. God's being in something is his reaching it by operation, and he neither operates on nor conserves non-being.
claims: God does not operate on or conserve non-being.

pgb1q29-d1e3573.summary: A further corollary, also labelled 'second'. Though God is necessarily everywhere, he is not beyond the heavens in an imaginary void. The void is pure nothing, and God is not in nothing.
claims: God is not present in the imaginary void beyond the heavens.
The void is pure nothing.

pgb1q29-d1e3598.summary: Third corollary. As God can cease to be everywhere, he can also begin to be everywhere, by destroying and recreating all places. God was not everywhere from eternity but began to be through creation, so he can be everywhere many times over.
claims: God's ubiquity began with creation.
God could cease to be and begin again to be everywhere.

pgb1q29-d1e3621.summary: Final corollary. Being everywhere many times does not make God composite or composable, and his 'passing' from place to place or time to time does not make him variable, for the same reason. Gracilis concludes that the affirmative part of the question follows.
claims: God's repeated ubiquity implies no composition or change in him.
The question is answered affirmatively.

pgb1q29-d1e3637.summary: Objection against the first conclusion. God can produce something beyond the heavens and so is there by power, but is not there by essence. So God can be somewhere by power without being there by essence.
claims: God can be somewhere by power but not by essence.

pgb1q29-d1e3645.summary: Objection against the second corollary of the first conclusion. If God could not act at a distance he would be less perfect than created agents, since acting at a distance is a perfection.
claims: Acting at a distance is a perfection.

pgb1q29-d1e3661.summary: Further objection to the same corollary. The divine will can will something distant from itself. Will and power are formally the same in God, so divine power can produce something distant from itself.
claims: Divine will and power are formally identical.

pgb1q29-d1e3669.summary: Objection against the second conclusion and corollaries. God can come to be where he was not and cease to be where he was, so he is mutable. If place b is destroyed, God is no longer there. If a new place is created, God is newly present to it. If God destroyed the outermost heaven or created a body beyond it, his location would change.
claims: God can gain and lose places and so is changeable.

pgb1q29-sphcnc.summary: An anticipated reply to the preceding objection: the change in such cases lies not in God but in the body newly created beyond the heavens.
claims: The change lies in the creature, not in God.

pgb1q29-d1e3700.summary: Rejoinder to the anticipated reply. Local motion is being here now and elsewhere before. The newly created body was nowhere before and did not arrive, so the local change must be God's. Confirmation: if God is there only through the body, the body is naturally prior to God's being there and could exist there without him. Also, God is naturally present somewhere before acting there.
claims: A newly created body undergoes no local motion.
God is naturally present before he acts.

pgb1q29-d1e3726.summary: First objection against the third conclusion and its corollaries. If God is not in the void beyond the heavens but can come to be there without positing a new body, he is locally mutable. God could place an angel with a body there and then annihilate the body while keeping the angel, as he could annihilate the air in a house while conserving us.
claims: God could come to be beyond the heavens without a new body there.

pgb1q29-d1e3769.summary: Second objection. Before the world's creation God was present to an imaginable space beyond the heavens. His acting in a space presupposes his presence there, he could have created the world before he did, and he could create another world beyond the outermost heaven.
claims: God's acting in a space presupposes his presence there.

pgb1q29-d1e3785.summary: Third objection. God knows distinctly and intuitively the infinite space beyond the heavens, and whatever God understands is actually present to him unless it is merely potential. So he is present to that space.
claims: Whatever God intuitively knows is actually present to him.

pgb1q29-d1e3794.summary: Fourth objection, from Augustine (De civ. Dei XI.5). Augustine answers those who ask why God created at this time rather than earlier by asking why he created in this place rather than elsewhere in infinite space. He calls it absurd to say God's substance is absent from infinite spaces beyond the world and confined to its small place. This seems to place God in extramundane space.
claims: Augustine seems to place God in infinite extramundane space.

pgb1q29-d1e3836.summary: Fifth objection, a thought experiment. Let a be the world's site and b a similar imaginary site beyond the heavens, and let God move the world from a to b. Either God was already in b, or by parity he is not now in a and would have moved from a to b, which is false. So God is now in b as in a.
claims: If God could move the world, he must already be present in the imaginary site.

pgb1q29-d1e3901.summary: Reply to the objection against the first conclusion. Saying God can act somewhere beyond the heavens is improper, since there is no 'where' or place there. 'God can act there' differs from 'God can act'. Or: wherever God can act, the divine essence is present.
claims: There is no place beyond the heavens.
Wherever God can act, his essence is present.

pgb1q29-d1e3917.summary: Reply to the second objection. In limited causes, inability to act at a distance comes from imperfection. In an unlimited cause it comes from perfection: divine immensity, simplicity, and immobility.
claims: God's inability to act at a distance follows from his perfection.

pgb1q29-d1e3928.summary: Reply to the third objection. The divine will cannot will anything distant from itself, for the same reasons of immensity, simplicity, and immobility.
claims: Nothing willed by God is distant from him.

pgb1q29-d1e3937.summary: Reply to the objection against the second conclusion. Something can come to be where it was not in two ways: by moving to a pre-existing place, or by the creation of the thing that is the place. God becomes newly present or ceases to be present in the second way, by a change in the place and not in himself. God does not leave a place; the place leaves God by ceasing to be.
claims: God's new presence results from change in the place, not in God.
When a place is destroyed, the place deserts God, not God the place.

pgb1q29-d1e3959.summary: Reply to the rejoinder. The newly created body does not move from place to place, but it does change, passing from non-being to being simpliciter. That is enough to account for God's new presence without change in God.
claims: Creation is a change from non-being to being sufficient to ground new relations.

pgb1q29-d1e3967.summary: Reply to the second rejoinder. God is not there through the body, nor by reason of it, if that implies the body causes something in God. In terms of necessary concomitance, God's being there is neither prior nor posterior to the body. In the order of natural understanding, though, the body's being and God's being are prior to God's being present to the body.
claims: The body does not cause God's presence.
God's presence to a body is conceptually posterior to the being of both.

pgb1q29-d1e3988.summary: Note: in the imaginary space beyond the heavens there is no 'here' or 'elsewhere' except potentially, since a magnitude could exist there in which different 'theres' would formally be.
claims: Extramundane space has only potential places.

pgb1q29-d1e4002.summary: Reply to the first objection against the third conclusion. If 'without new positing' means without any present or past positing, the objection's antecedent is denied. If it means only without a body now existing there, the inference is denied: God's becoming present involves some present or past change in a creature. The angel case shows only that God can be beyond the heavens once some creature is posited there, whether or not it remains, not with nothing ever posited. The change is in the angel, just as God cannot go from not loving b to loving b without a change in b. This reflects God's immutability, a perfection.
claims: God's new presence always involves some present or past change in a creature.
God cannot begin to love something without a change in it.

pgb1q29-d1e4056.summary: Second reply to the same objection. God is not said to be in the imaginable space beyond the heavens because nothing is, was, or will be there. It would be pointless to posit God throughout an infinite space where he never acts.
claims: It is idle to posit God in a space where nothing exists or is done.

pgb1q29-d1e4074.summary: Reply to the second objection. Gracilis denies that God was present to a space before creation. That space was pure nothing, and God was in himself.
claims: Before creation, God was in himself, not in any space.

pgb1q29-d1e4082.summary: Further reply to the second objection. God's actually acting beyond the heavens should not be posited unless reason or authority compels it. Divine immensity does not demand it. It demands only that no place or thing can exist outside and distant from God without his being present to it by essence, power, and intuition, which God has of himself.
claims: Divine immensity requires only that God be present to whatever exists.
God's extramundane action should not be posited without compelling reason or authority.

pgb1q29-d1e4092.summary: Third reply to the second objection. Even if a creature could by God's power be everywhere, it could be absent from some existing place and does not have ubiquity of itself. God, by his immensity, cannot be absent from anything while it exists.
claims: A creature's ubiquity would be accidental and derived.
God's ubiquity flows from his immensity.

pgb1q29-d1e4110.summary: Reply to the third objection. As God was not actually present to time when nothing existed, so he is not present to a space that is nothing. His knowledge of such space does not entail presence to it.
claims: Knowledge of an imaginary space does not entail presence to it.

pgb1q29-d1e4119.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Augustine argues against those who imagine infinite time before creation and, correspondingly, infinite space around the world, and who ask why God chose this time or place. His point is that by their reasoning they would have to posit infinitely many worlds. He is attacking the idea of an actual spatial receptacle for bodies, which in truth is no more than a chimera.
claims: Augustine's remark is ad hominem against believers in infinite space and time.
Actual extramundane space is a chimera.

pgb1q29-d1e4179.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. Gracilis admits the setup but says b is not like a, since a is real being and b is not. B is not distant from a, because there is no distance between being and non-being. And God could not move the world to the imaginary site, since motion cannot acquire a place in a void or terminate in non-being.
claims: There is no distance between being and non-being.
The world cannot be moved into imaginary space.

pgb1q29-d1e4233.summary: Closing remark: the replies to the principal arguments are evident from the conclusions.

pgb1q29-d1e4237.summary: Opens a list of the conclusions of distinction 37, restating Lombard's teaching. First conclusion: God, always existing immutably in himself, is in every nature by presence, power, and essence. He is in every place without circumscription and in every time without change. He dwells by grace in holy spirits and souls, and most excellently in Christ, in whom the fullness of the deity dwells bodily.
claims: God is in all things by presence, power, and essence.
God dwells by grace in the saints and most excellently in Christ.

pgb1q29-d1e4263.summary: Second conclusion. Wherever God dwells he is, but he does not dwell everywhere he is. As the soul is whole in every part of the body but acts more intensely in some, God is everywhere but is specially in the saints by grace, as in a temple. The wicked, though where God is, are not with him. 'Our Father who art in heaven' means in the saints.
claims: God's dwelling is narrower than his presence.
God dwells specially in the saints by grace.

pgb1q29-d1e4292.summary: Third conclusion. Before things existed God was in himself. Now he is in himself and in things. The saints are called God's house not as if God would fall without it, but because they would fall if he departed.
claims: God was in himself before creation.
Creatures depend on God's indwelling, not God on them.

pgb1q29-d1e4305.summary: Fourth conclusion. God dwells in some who do not know him, such as baptized infants, and in some who know him, such as the blessed who love him. He does not dwell in some who know him, the wicked who know but do not love or glorify him.
claims: Indwelling depends on love and grace, not on knowledge.

pgb1q29-d1e4319.summary: Fifth conclusion. As the sun's rays are not soiled by filth, the divine essence, though everywhere, is stained by no impurity.
claims: God's presence in impure things does not defile him.

pgb1q29-d1e4325.summary: Sixth conclusion, contrasting three modes of being in place. A body is local, in place by division (circumscriptively), and mobile in place and time. A created spirit is local not by division but determinately, being here and not elsewhere, and mobile in place and in time through changes of joy, sorrow, knowledge, and forgetting. God is not local and is uncircumscribable, whole everywhere, and wholly immobile.
claims: Bodies are in place circumscriptively, spirits definitively, and God neither.

pg-b1q29-Dd1e98.summary: Literal division of distinction 37. Moving from things' being in God's knowledge to God's being in the essence of things, Lombard approves true modes of divine presence, rejects false ones, and confirms his teaching. The first part distinguishes God's special presence by grace in the saints from his general presence by nature in all things.
claims: Distinction 37 treats God's being in things, both generally by nature and specially by grace.

pg-b1q29-Dd1e211.summary: Principal arguments. Against necessary divine ubiquity: God could then not act at a distance, and he might be everywhere by power only. God can acquire new places, and creatures are contingent. God can begin to be everywhere, is not in the imaginary void, and Christ as man is not everywhere. For it: the Master's authority, and ubiquity as a perfection.
claims: Against: action at a distance, divine acquisition of place, and the beginning of ubiquity.
For: ubiquity is a perfection.

pg-b1q29-Dd1e254.summary: First conclusion and corollaries. God cannot be anywhere by power without being there by essence, and against Scotus, power and essence are identical in God. So, unlike creatures, God cannot act at a distance, since nothing is distant from him. Ubiquity 'attinctive' through power and essence is proper to God. A creature could be everywhere only 'contentive', if all other places were annihilated.
claims: Presence by power entails presence by essence.
God cannot act at a distance.
Only God is everywhere attinctive.

pg-b1q29-Dd1e356.summary: Second conclusion and corollaries. God needs no place and is contained by none, since containment means being bounded and exceeded. Spatial and temporal predicates apply to God only by transference, yet his modes of being in creatures (by essence, presence, and power, after Gerard of Siena) are distinct. God can no more be circumscribed or moved than a creature can exist without his intimate presence. He is one way in himself and many ways in creatures, since presence-talk connotes his diverse effects, signifying immensity, grace, or union, as Alan of Lille says.
claims: No place contains God.
God is in things by essence, presence, and power.
Presence-talk about God connotes his effects in creatures.

pg-b1q29-Dd1e521.summary: Third conclusion and corollaries. God is necessarily in every existing creature but contingently in any given place, which could be annihilated. He is in nothing that does not exist, since presence is reaching a thing by essence, knowledge, and conserving operation. So he is not in the imaginary void beyond the heavens, which is pure nothing. His ubiquity began with creation and could cease and begin again, implying no composition or change in him. The affirmative answer to the question follows.
claims: God is necessarily in every existing creature.
God is not in the imaginary void.
God's ubiquity began with creation and implies no change in him.

pg-b1q29-Dd1e564.summary: Objections and replies, centred on whether God is in extramundane space and whether new presence means change in God. The objections: God acts beyond the heavens by power alone; acting at a distance is a perfection; God gains and loses places. A rejoinder adds that a newly created body does not move, so God must. Further objections draw on an angel left beyond the heavens, God's presence before creation, his intuitive knowledge of infinite space, Augustine's De civitate Dei XI.5, and moving the world into an imaginary site. The replies: there is no 'where' beyond the heavens; inability to act at a distance follows from immensity. New presence is a change in the creature (the place 'deserts God'), grounded in creation as a change from non-being to being, as God cannot begin to love b without a change in b. The imaginary space is pure nothing with only potential places, idle to fill with God. Augustine argues ad hominem against a chimerical infinite space. There is no distance between being and non-being.
claims: New divine presence is always a change in the creature, not in God.
Extramundane space is nothing and God is not present to it.
God cannot act at a distance because of his immensity, not from imperfection.

pg-b1q29-Dd1e200.summary: The question asks whether the divine necessary principle is necessarily in every being, and whether each thing is a mutable place capable of God. Gracilis answers affirmatively, with careful qualifications. God's presence by power entails presence by essence, against Scotus, because the two are identical in God, so God cannot act at a distance. No place contains or circumscribes God. His being in creatures, by essence, presence, and power, connotes his diverse effects in them. God is necessarily present to whatever exists but contingently in any particular place, and he is in nothing that does not exist, including the imaginary void beyond the heavens. Extensive replies defend this against arguments from extramundane action, from Augustine, and from thought experiments about moving the world. New divine presence is explained as a change in the creature alone, grounded in creation and God's immutability.
claims: God is necessarily present to every existing creature by essence, presence, and power.
God is not present in the imaginary void beyond the heavens.
Changes in God's presence are changes in creatures, not in God.
Divine presence by power entails presence by essence.

pg-b1q29-Dd1e889.summary: Conclusions of distinction 37, a summary of Lombard's text appended after the question. God, immutable in himself, is in all things by presence, power, and essence, uncircumscribed in place and unchanged in time. He dwells by grace in the saints and most excellently in Christ. Dwelling is narrower than presence, as with the soul in the body. God was in himself before creation, and the saints depend on his indwelling rather than he on them. Indwelling follows love, not knowledge. God's presence in impure things does not defile him. Bodies are in place circumscriptively, created spirits determinately, and God neither, being wholly immobile.
claims: God is in all things by presence, power, and essence.
Indwelling by grace is narrower than presence and follows love.
Bodies, spirits, and God are in place in distinct ways.

pg-b1q29.summary: Lectio 29, on distinction 37 of Book I: God's being in things. The exposition presents Lombard's distinction as moving from things' being in God's knowledge to God's being in things, generally by nature and specially by grace. The question asks whether God, as necessary principle, is necessarily in every being. Gracilis answers that God is necessarily present by essence, presence, and power to whatever exists, but contingently in any given place. Against Scotus, presence by power entails presence by essence, so God cannot act at a distance. No place contains him, and presence-talk connotes his diverse effects. A long exchange of objections and replies denies that God is present in the imaginary void beyond the heavens, reads Augustine's appeal to infinite space as ad hominem, and treats all new divine presence as change in the creature alone. A closing list of the distinction's conclusions restates Lombard's teaching: God's indwelling by grace, in the saints and supremely in Christ, and the distinct ways bodies, spirits, and God are in place.
claims: God is necessarily present to every existing creature by essence, presence, and power.
God is not present in the imaginary void beyond the heavens.
Changes in God's presence are changes in creatures alone.
God dwells by grace in the saints and most excellently in Christ.
